tldr: The authors propose KareCoder, a knowledge-aware code generation framework that integrates an algorithm and data structure knowledge library into LLM reasoning, achieving a 23.3% relative improvement on Pass@1 over ChatGPT on novel programming competition problems.
contributions: Constructed CodeF, a Python programming competition dataset of 1523 problems sourced from Codeforces, split by ChatGPT's September 2021 training cutoff into CodeF pre2021-9 (805 problems) and CodeF post2021-9 (718 problems)
Developed a Knowledge Library containing 33 algorithm and data structure categories in three formats: knowledge description, pseudo-code, and step-by-step pseudo-code explanation
Proposed KareCoder, a two-stage approach comprising a Prompt Engineering stage (knowledge-aware prompt generation via dictionary matching) and a Coding stage (code generation guided by the prompt)
methods: The authors built CodeF by crawling Codeforces with a custom HTML parser, then de-commented code via AST parsing, deduplicated using MinHash and Jaccard index (threshold 0.85), and validated with unit tests. A tag generator based on ChatGPT was designed for problems lacking algorithm tags. The Knowledge Library was manually compiled from resources including Competitive Programmer's Handbook and reviewed by seven industry professionals. KareCoder operates in two stages: first, dictionary matching retrieves relevant knowledge from the library based on problem tags to generate a one-shot knowledge-aware prompt; second, ChatGPT acts as a coder to generate executable Python code guided by that prompt.
results: On the CodeF dataset, KareCoder achieved a 23.3% relative improvement on the Pass@1 metric compared to code directly generated by ChatGPT. The approach demonstrated outstanding performance on novel problems previously unencountered by LLMs. Evaluation was also conducted on the APPS dataset.
limitations: The Knowledge Library covers only 33 algorithm and data structure categories and is tailored specifically to Python programming contest problems, limiting generalizability to other languages or broader problem domains. The one-shot examples were manually curated by eight students and may not generalize across all problem types. The approach relies on accurate tag matching, which could fail if tag prediction is incorrect.
